title: runc
explain: runc is the low-level runtime behind Docker, containerd and Kubernetes that turns an image into a running Linux process walled in by two kernel features: namespaces limit what the process can see, cgroups limit how much it can use. It is essentially native speed with the highest density, but the process still makes ordinary syscalls into the shared host kernel, so the kernel is the boundary. (Namespace 管看见什么, cgroup 管用多少.)
model:
A container is a **process tree** (not a VM, and not a single thread) on the host kernel, fenced by:

| Mechanism | Controls | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Namespaces** | what it can *see* | pid, mnt (root fs), net, uts (hostname), ipc, user |
| **cgroups** | what it can *use* | CPU, memory, number of processes, I/O |
| Extras | what it may *do* | dropped capabilities, seccomp syscall filter, AppArmor/SELinux, read-only or overlay root fs |

```
app process ──syscall──▶  SHARED HOST KERNEL  ◀── neighbour containers
   (own pid/mnt/net view, cgroup limits, seccomp filter)
```

**Boundary:** the kernel's own enforcement. One kernel bug or runtime escape (such as CVE-2019-5736) can reach the host and every neighbour.

**Overhead:** near zero. No guest kernel, no extra memory, starts in tens of milliseconds.

**Pick it** for your own or semi-trusted code, CI and microservices. For hostile multi-tenant code step up to [gVisor](#/sd/f/gvisor), a microVM or [WASM](#/sd/f/wasm). Compare [native sandboxes](#/sd/f/native-sandboxes) and [tenant isolation](#/sd/f/tenant-isolation).

details.q: What do namespaces and cgroups each do?
details.a: Namespaces give the process its own view: its own process tree, mounts and root filesystem, network stack, hostname, IPC and user ids. Cgroups meter and cap its consumption of CPU, memory, process count and I/O. Visibility and consumption are separate: a pid namespace hides other processes but does not stop a fork bomb.

details.q: A container runs a fork bomb and starves the node of process slots. What should have stopped it?
details.a: The pids cgroup limit, which caps how many processes the container can create. The pid namespace only changes numbering and visibility. This is why 'it is in a container' is not a resource guarantee until limits are set.

details.q: Is a container a lightweight VM?
details.a: No. A VM boots its own kernel on virtualized hardware. A container is ordinary processes on the host kernel with restricted view and quotas. That is why it starts fast and packs densely, and also why a kernel bug inside a container is a bug in the host.

details.q: What is the main residual risk when you run customer code in runc with the default seccomp profile?
details.a: Every allowed syscall still reaches the shared host kernel, which has a very large attack surface. A vulnerability reachable through any allowed call, or a bug in the runtime, can lead to host compromise. A VM adds a hardware-enforced boundary and a separate guest kernel.

details.q: Is root inside the container root on the host?
details.a: Without a user namespace, uid 0 in the container is uid 0 on the host, though with reduced capabilities and seccomp. Rootless containers or user namespaces map container root to an unprivileged host uid, shrinking the damage of an escape.

details.q: How many sandboxes fit on a node?
details.a: Divide allocatable memory by the per-sandbox hard limit. A 64 GiB node with 2 GiB reserved for the OS and agents, at 512 MiB per sandbox, gives (62 x 1024) / 512 = 124. Density this high is runc's strength; a VM per sandbox pays a guest-kernel cost each.

details.q: Rank the isolation options by strength against a kernel exploit.
details.a: Weakest to strongest: a plain non-root process, a runc container with seccomp and dropped capabilities, gVisor (a user-space kernel answering the syscalls), then a microVM with its own guest kernel behind the hypervisor. Overhead rises in the same order.

prompts.q: Explain what a container really is and what isolates it.
points: A process tree on the shared host kernel, not a VM or a thread
Namespaces limit what it can see
Cgroups limit what it can use
Seccomp, capabilities and AppArmor limit what it may do
Image root filesystem is overlay or read-only

prompts.q: Is runc enough to run untrusted customer code? Justify.
points: The host kernel is shared, so syscalls are the attack surface
A kernel or runtime bug can escape to host and neighbours
Hardening helps: seccomp, rootless, user namespaces
Fine for own or semi-trusted code
Step up to gVisor, microVM or WASM for hostile code

prompts.q: Place runc among the sandbox options on the cost versus strength curve.
points: runc: near-native speed, highest density, weakest of the container options
WASM: fast start, must compile to WASM
microVM: strongest, heavier start and memory
Native MAC sandboxes as hardening, not tenant isolation
